The revelation calls today a day of sacrifice and tithing, and says great things come from small things. It ends by saying the Lord requires the heart and a willing mind, and that Zion will flourish.
dc-64.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 11 September 1831. He was preparing to move to Hiram to resume his Bible revision. Some who went to Missouri that summer came back disappointed. Ezra Booth had turned against Joseph Smith, and on 6 September a conference barred Booth from preaching. Edward Partridge had also clashed with Joseph Smith in Missouri over the land being bought.

verse.text: I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.

dc-65.summary: The revelation describes a mighty voice from on high calling people to “prepare ye the way of the Lord” and make his paths straight. It says the keys of the kingdom of God are committed to men on earth. From there the gospel will roll forth like the stone cut from the mountain without hands. The voice calls people to prepare the supper of the Lamb and make ready for the Bridegroom. It tells them to pray and make known the Lord’s works. They are to call on the Lord so his kingdom may go forth. It says the Son of Man will come down to meet the kingdom of God set up on earth. The section ends as a prayer that the kingdom of God go forth so the kingdom of heaven may come.
dc-65.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Hiram, Ohio, on 30 October 1831. It may have come during a Sunday meeting at the home of John and Elsa Johnson. William E. McLellin, who preached there that day, made an early copy. He linked it to the request “Thy kingdom come” in the Lord’s Prayer. The scribe of the original is unknown.

verse.text: The keys of the kingdom of God are committed unto man on the earth, and from thence shall the gospel roll forth unto the ends of the earth, as the stone which is cut out of the mountain without hands shall roll forth, until it has filled the whole earth.

dc-66.summary: The voice in verse 1 speaks as the Redeemer to William McLellin and blesses him for turning from his sins and receiving the everlasting covenant. It says he is clean, “but not all,” and must repent of what the Lord will show him. He is to preach from land to land where the gospel has not been heard. He is not to go to Zion yet, but to the eastern lands with Samuel Smith. He is to lay hands on the sick, be patient in affliction, and not be cumbered. It warns him against adultery, a temptation that has troubled him. If he continues to the end, he will receive a crown of eternal life.
dc-66.setting: William E. McLellin, a recent convert from Paris, Illinois, met Joseph Smith at a conference in Orange, Ohio, on 25–26 October 1831. He then traveled with Joseph to Hiram, arriving on 29 October. McLellin had privately asked the Lord five questions, which he never recorded. At his request, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation that day, probably in the John Johnson home. McLellin wrote it down and said it answered his questions fully.

verse.text: Verily I say unto you, my servant William, that you are clean, but not all; repent, therefore, of those things which are not pleasing in my sight, saith the Lord, for the Lord will show them unto you.

dc-67.summary: The revelation speaks to the assembled elders and says their prayers have been heard. It says fears in their hearts kept them from a blessing they sought. It notes they have watched Joseph Smith’s language and imperfections. It then sets a test: pick the least revelation and let the wisest elder write one like it. If they can, they may say they do not know the revelations are true. If they cannot, they are condemned unless they testify. It closes with a promise that the humble will one day see God by the Spirit.
dc-67.setting: Elders met in conference at Hiram, Ohio, on 1–2 November 1831. They voted to publish Joseph Smith’s revelations as the Book of Commandments. Several elders signed a statement that the revelations came by inspiration. Some held back, partly over doubts about the plain language Joseph used. Joseph dictated this revelation during the conference, but the exact day is uncertain. His later history says William McLellin then tried to write a revelation and failed.

verse.text: Or, if there be any among you that shall make one like unto it, then ye are justified in saying that ye do not know that they are true;

dc-68.summary: The revelation begins with Orson Hyde’s call to preach by the Spirit. It makes his call a pattern for all who are ordained to go forth. Whatever they speak when moved by the Holy Ghost will be scripture. It sends Hyde, Luke Johnson, Lyman Johnson, and William McLellin into all the world to preach and baptize. It then gives rules for bishops, including the rights of literal descendants of Aaron. Parents in Zion must teach their children faith, repentance, baptism, and the Holy Ghost by age eight. The Lord says he is displeased with idlers and greed in Zion. Oliver Cowdery is to carry these sayings there.
dc-68.setting: This revelation is dated 1 November 1831, at Hiram, Ohio, during the conference on publishing the revelations. Orson Hyde, Luke Johnson, Lyman Johnson, and William McLellin asked Joseph Smith to learn the Lord’s will for them. The first part answers them, and the rest speaks to the whole church. It may first have been two revelations later copied together. In 1835 Joseph Smith expanded the text for the Doctrine and Covenants. The added passages concern who may serve as bishop and how bishops are appointed.

verse.text: And whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture, shall be the will of the Lord, shall be the mind of the Lord, shall be the word of the Lord, shall be the voice of the Lord, and the power of God unto salvation.

dc-69.summary: The revelation says Oliver Cowdery should not travel alone with the commandments and the money. It names John Whitmer to go with him. Whitmer is to keep writing a history of important things about the church. He is to take counsel from Cowdery and others. Elders abroad are to send accounts of their stewardships to Zion. Zion is to be the place that receives these things. Whitmer is also to travel among the churches to gather knowledge and records. The work is for the generations who will grow up in Zion.
dc-69.setting: Oliver Cowdery was assigned to carry the compiled revelations to Independence, Missouri, for printing. He was also to take money donated for the church there. On 11 November 1831, at Hiram, Ohio, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation. It sent John Whitmer, the church historian, with him. The two left for Missouri on 20 November. The Joseph Smith Papers editors call the date probable but not certain.

verse.text: And also that he shall continue in writing and making a history of all the important things which he shall observe and know concerning my church;

dc-70.summary: The revelation speaks to Zion and to church members far away. It appoints six men as stewards over the revelations: Joseph Smith, Martin Harris, Oliver Cowdery, John Whitmer, Sidney Rigdon, and William W. Phelps. They will give an account of this stewardship at judgment. They are to manage the revelations and their benefits, not give them away. What exceeds their needs goes to the Lord’s storehouse for Zion. No one is exempt from this law, not even the bishop. Stewards over spiritual things deserve support, and all must be equal in temporal things.
dc-70.setting: A series of conferences at Hiram, Ohio, ended on 12 November 1831. The last one voted that the revelations were worth the riches of the whole earth to the church. Joseph Smith asked the elders to support those who had worked on the church’s sacred writings. He dictated this revelation that day, possibly in answer to a question. The exact question is not recorded.

verse.text: Nevertheless, in your temporal things you shall be equal, and this not grudgingly, otherwise the abundance of the manifestations of the Spirit shall be withheld.

dc-71.summary: The revelation tells Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon that the time has come to preach. They are to expound the scriptures by the Spirit given them. They are to preach in the nearby regions and in the church for a season. This work will prepare the way for revelations still to come. They are to invite their enemies to meet them in public and in private. If they are faithful, their critics’ shame will be shown. The revelation promises that no weapon formed against them will prosper. It closes by telling them to keep the commandments.
dc-71.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were revising the Bible at the John Johnson home in Hiram, Ohio. Ezra Booth, a former member, had published critical letters in the Ohio Star of Ravenna since October 1831. Symonds Rider, also disaffected, had given a February 1831 revelation to another local paper. On 1 December 1831, Joseph dictated this revelation, which set the Bible work aside so both men could preach. Rigdon later challenged both critics to public meetings, and both declined.

verse.text: Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you—there is no weapon that is formed against you shall prosper;

dc-72.summary: The first revelation tells the high priests at Kirtland that a bishop is needed in this region. Elders here must account for their stewardship to him, with records sent to the bishop in Zion. It names Newel K. Whitney as that bishop. The second revelation sets his duties: keep the storehouse, receive funds, and supply the elders. Debts elders cannot pay go to the bishop in Zion, and their spiritual labors answer for them. Elders need this bishop’s certificate to be accepted in Zion, and publishing stewards may claim his help. The third requires members moving to Zion to carry a certificate from three elders or a bishop.
dc-72.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon traveled from Hiram to Kirtland, Ohio, on 3 December 1831. The next day high priests and members met there to learn their duties. Joseph dictated three revelations that day, later printed together as this section. The first called the Kirtland merchant Newel K. Whitney as bishop in Ohio, while Edward Partridge served as bishop in Missouri. The other two set Whitney’s duties and rules for moving to Zion.

verse.text: And verily in this thing ye have done wisely, for it is required of the Lord, at the hand of every steward, to render an account of his stewardship, both in time and in eternity.

dc-73.summary: The revelation says the elders should keep preaching in the nearby regions until the conference. At the conference their separate missions will be made known. It then tells Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to translate again. They should also preach nearby until the conference when it is practical. After that they are to continue translating until the work is finished. This plan is a pattern for the elders until more is revealed. It ends by telling them to gird up their loins and be sober.
dc-73.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon had preached around Hiram and Kirtland, Ohio, since early December 1831. A later history says their preaching calmed feelings stirred by Ezra Booth’s published letters. They returned to Hiram about 8 January 1832. On 10 January, Joseph dictated this revelation in the John Johnson home, probably with Rigdon as scribe. A general conference was due about two weeks later.

verse.text: And, inasmuch as it is practicable, to preach in the regions round about until conference; and after that it is expedient to continue the work of translation until it be finished.

dc-74.summary: The explanation opens by quoting Paul: an unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing one. It says that in the apostles’ day unbelieving Jews still kept the law of circumcision. Contention arose when unbelieving husbands wanted their children circumcised under the law of Moses. Those children followed their fathers’ traditions and did not believe the gospel. So Paul wrote, on his own authority, that believers should not marry unbelievers. His aim was to end the tradition that little children are unholy. It concludes that little children are holy, sanctified through the atonement of Jesus Christ.
dc-74.setting: John Whitmer copied this explanation of scripture into Revelation Book 1 and dated it only 1830. He gave the place as Wayne County, New York, so it predates Joseph Smith’s move to Ohio in January 1831. Later histories wrongly placed it in January 1832. It explains 1 Corinthians 7:14, a verse often used to support infant baptism. The official heading ties it to questions about baptism, but the exact occasion is not recorded.

verse.text: But little children are holy, being sanctified through the atonement of Jesus Christ; and this is what the scriptures mean.

dc-75.summary: The first revelation tells those who volunteered to preach to go without delay and labor with their might. Faithful workers are promised sheaves, honor, and eternal life. William McLellin’s eastern mission is revoked; he is chastened for murmuring, forgiven, and sent south with Luke Johnson. Orson Hyde, Samuel Smith, Lyman Johnson, and Orson Pratt go east, and other pairs go west and south. Houses that reject them are to be left with the dust shaken off as a testimony. The second revelation asks the church to support the families of those sent out. A man who must provide for his own family may stay and keep his crown, but idlers have no place. It ends by pairing fourteen more men, including Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Ezra Thayre.
dc-75.setting: A general conference met at Amherst, Ohio, on 25 January 1832, about fifty miles west of Kirtland. William McLellin later said seventy to eighty church officers attended. Joseph Smith was ordained President of the High Priesthood there. Elders who had offered to preach asked to know the Lord’s will for them. Joseph dictated two revelations that day, now verses 1–22 and 23–36. The 1835 Doctrine and Covenants combined them into one section.

verse.text: And again, verily I say unto you, that every man who is obliged to provide for his own family, let him provide, and he shall in nowise lose his crown; and let him labor in the church.

dc-76.summary: The text opens with praise and a promise to reveal mysteries to the faithful. Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon then testify that they saw the Son at the Father’s right hand. They report the fall of Lucifer and the fate of the sons of perdition, who alone are not redeemed. The vision describes the celestial glory, like the sun, for those who receive Christ’s testimony, are baptized, and overcome by faith. The terrestrial glory, like the moon, is for the honorable who were not valiant in that testimony. The telestial glory, like the stars, is for those who did not receive the gospel but did not deny the Holy Spirit. Its inhabitants are numberless, and all will bow to Christ. The writers say they saw more than they were allowed to write.
dc-76.setting: Joseph Smith returned from the Amherst conference and resumed revising the Bible at the John Johnson home in Hiram, Ohio. Sidney Rigdon was his scribe. Joseph had reasoned that heaven must hold more than one kingdom if people are judged by their deeds. On 16 February 1832, while pondering John 5:29, the two reported seeing a vision together. Philo Dibble later said about twelve men were in the room, but his accounts vary. The vision was printed in The Evening and the Morning Star in July 1832.

verse.text: And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!

dc-77.summary: The section is a list of fifteen questions and answers about Revelation chapters 4 to 11. It says the sea of glass is the earth in its sanctified, eternal state. It says the four beasts were four individual beasts shown to John, representing classes of beings in their glory. Their eyes stand for knowledge and their wings for power. The book with seven seals holds God’s works for the earth’s seven thousand years, one seal for each thousand. The angel from the east and the little book John ate are both tied to Elias, who gathers Israel and restores all things. The trumpets prepare the way for Christ’s coming at the start of the seventh thousand years. The two witnesses are two prophets sent to the Jews after they rebuild Jerusalem.
dc-77.setting: Joseph Smith was revising the New Testament in early 1832 and reached the book of Revelation. He was living at Hiram, Ohio, in the home of John and Elsa Johnson. His later history says he received an explanation of John’s Revelation about the start of March. The Joseph Smith Papers date the document to between about 4 and 20 March 1832. Sidney Rigdon or Jesse Gause probably wrote it down.

verse.text: Q. What are we to understand by the book which John saw, which was sealed on the back with seven seals? A. We are to understand that it contains the revealed will, mysteries, and the works of God; the hidden things of his economy concerning this earth during the seven thousand years of its continuance, or its temporal existence.

dc-78.summary: The revelation tells high priests in council that the time has come to organize the storehouse for the poor in Kirtland and Zion. It states that if they are not equal in earthly things, they cannot be equal in obtaining heavenly things. It names Newel K. Whitney, Joseph Smith, and Sidney Rigdon to sit in council with the Saints in Zion. It commands them to bind themselves by an everlasting covenant, and whoever breaks it loses office and standing. It names Michael as prince, holding keys under the Holy One. It calls them little children who cannot bear all things yet. Still, it promises to lead them along. It closes by promising that the faithful and wise steward will inherit all things.
dc-78.setting: Joseph Smith came to Kirtland, Ohio, from his home in Hiram on 1 March 1832. He met with high priests about the Church’s publishing and store businesses and dictated this revelation there. Sidney Gilbert had opened a store in Independence, partly funded by Newel K. Whitney of Kirtland. It led to the United Firm, organized in April 1832 and dissolved in 1834. Later editions replaced “firm” and the business terms with “order” and the storehouse for the poor.

verse.text: For if ye are not equal in earthly things ye cannot be equal in obtaining heavenly things;

dc-79.summary: The revelation tells Jared Carter to go again into the eastern countries. He is to preach from city to city by the authority of his ordination. It promises to send the Comforter to teach him the truth and where to go. If he is faithful, he will be crowned “again with sheaves.” It tells him to let his heart be glad and not to fear. The speaker names himself as Jesus Christ.
dc-79.setting: Jared Carter had spent late 1831 and early 1832 preaching in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, and Vermont. A few weeks after returning home to Amherst, Ohio, he went to Hiram. There he asked Joseph Smith what the Lord wanted for his next season of preaching. Joseph dictated this revelation on 12 March 1832. Carter left on the new mission on 15 April 1832.

verse.text: And I will send upon him the Comforter, which shall teach him the truth and the way whither he shall go;

dc-80.summary: The revelation tells Stephen Burnett to go into the world and preach to all who hear his voice. Because he wants a companion, it gives him Eden Smith. It says they “cannot go amiss” whether they go north, south, east, or west. It tells them to declare what they have heard, believe, and know to be true. It closes by naming the one who calls them as Jesus Christ.
dc-80.setting: Stephen Burnett was a young Ohio convert, ordained a high priest at seventeen in October 1831. A January 1832 revelation paired him with Ruggles Eames, but it is unclear whether they served. On 7 March 1832, at Hiram, Ohio, Joseph Smith dictated this new call. Eden Smith fell ill that same day, so the two did not preach together until August 1832. One manuscript copy dates it 17 March, but editors favor 7 March.

verse.text: Therefore, declare the things which ye have heard, and verily believe, and know to be true.

dc-81.summary: The revelation calls Frederick G. Williams to be a high priest and a counselor to Joseph Smith. It says Joseph holds the keys of the kingdom, which belong to the Presidency of the High Priesthood. It promises blessings if the counselor is faithful in counsel, in prayer, and in preaching. It asks for prayer both vocally and in the heart, in public and in private. It tells him to succor the weak, lift up hands that hang down, and strengthen feeble knees. If he is faithful to the end, he will receive a crown of immortality and eternal life.
dc-81.setting: Joseph Smith had been ordained President of the High Priesthood at Amherst, Ohio, in January 1832. On 8 March he chose Jesse Gause and Sidney Rigdon as counselors. This revelation, dated 15 March 1832 at Hiram, was first addressed to Gause. Gause did not continue faithfully and was excommunicated in December 1832. Frederick G. Williams’s name later replaced his, and Williams was ordained a counselor on 18 March 1833.

verse.text: Wherefore, be faithful; stand in the office which I have appointed unto you; succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.

dc-82.summary: The revelation first tells the men that as they forgive each other, the Lord forgives them. It warns that all have sinned and that much is required of those given much. It says, “I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say,” but disobedience brings no promise. It names Edward Partridge, Newel K. Whitney, Sidney Gilbert, Sidney Rigdon, Joseph Smith, John Whitmer, Oliver Cowdery, W. W. Phelps, and Martin Harris. They are to be bound by a covenant in their stewardships over the poor and the bishopric. Their work covers both Zion and Kirtland, which the revelation calls a stake to Zion. Each has equal claims on the properties by just wants and needs, and surplus goes to the Lord’s storehouse. It ends with counsel to make friends with the “mammon of unrighteousness” and leave judgment to God.
dc-82.setting: Joseph Smith traveled to Missouri in April 1832 with Sidney Rigdon, Newel K. Whitney, and Jesse Gause. On 26 April a council of high priests and elders met in Independence. The council sustained Joseph as President of the High Priesthood. It also settled a dispute between Sidney Rigdon and Edward Partridge. Joseph dictated this revelation that afternoon, renewing the March call to form the United Firm.

verse.text: For of him unto whom much is given much is required; and he who sins against the greater light shall receive the greater condemnation.

dc-83.summary: The revelation adds to the Church’s laws for women and children who have lost husbands or fathers. Wives have a claim on their husbands for support until the husbands die. Faithful widows keep fellowship in the Church; unfaithful ones lose it but may stay on their inheritances under the law of the land. Children have a claim on their parents until they come of age. After that, they have a claim on the Lord’s storehouse if their parents cannot give them inheritances. The storehouse is kept by consecrations, and it provides for widows, orphans, and the poor.
dc-83.setting: On 30 April 1832, Joseph Smith sat in council with Church leaders in Independence, Missouri. Days earlier he had visited the Colesville Saints in Kaw Township, about twelve miles west. That settlement included widows such as Phebe Peck and Anna Rogers. The Joseph Smith Papers editors think contact with these families likely raised a question. Under consecration, what claim did a widow have on property her husband had given the Church?

verse.text: And if they are not faithful they shall not have fellowship in the church; yet they may remain upon their inheritances according to the laws of the land.

dc-84.summary: The revelation says the New Jerusalem and its temple will be built at the temple lot in western Missouri, within “this generation” of people. It traces the greater priesthood from Moses through Jethro, Abraham, Melchizedek, Noah, and Enoch back to Adam. It says this priesthood holds the key of the knowledge of God, and its ordinances show the power of godliness. Because Israel hardened their hearts under Moses, the higher priesthood was taken, and the lesser one continued until John the Baptist. It describes the oath and covenant of the priesthood: those who receive it receive Christ, the Father, and all the Father has. It says the whole church is under condemnation for treating lightly the Book of Mormon and the commandments. It sends the elders, called apostles and friends, to preach without purse or scrip, and warns cities that reject them. It assigns Bishop Newel K. Whitney to warn New York, Albany, and Boston, and ends with a promise of the Lord’s coming.
dc-84.setting: Joseph Smith moved from Hiram to Kirtland, Ohio, on 12 September 1832. Elders were returning from missions in the eastern states to report on their work. Joseph inquired of the Lord with six of them, and the revelation came over the night of 22–23 September. It was probably dictated in Newel K. Whitney’s store, with Frederick G. Williams as scribe. Partway through, the text shifts to address ten high priests.

verse.text: Therefore, in the ordinances thereof, the power of godliness is manifest.

dc-85.summary: The letter says the Lord’s clerk must keep a history and record of all that happens in Zion. The record lists those who consecrate property and receive inheritances, with their faith and works. Those who do not receive inheritances by consecration are not to be enrolled with God’s people. Their genealogy is not to be kept in the Church’s records. Joseph Smith then quotes what he calls the still small voice. It says God will send one “mighty and strong” to set the house in order and divide inheritances by lot. The man who steadies the ark will fall, and those not written in the book will have no inheritance among the Saints.
dc-85.setting: Joseph Smith returned to Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 November 1832 after a trip east with Newel K. Whitney. On 27 November he wrote a letter to William W. Phelps in Independence, Missouri. Phelps had reported in print that 810 Saints had moved to Zion and asked whether all had kept the law. Some had arrived without consecrating property and so had no inheritance from the bishop. This section is an extract of that letter, printed in January 1833 and added to the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.

verse.text: It is contrary to the will and commandment of God that those who receive not their inheritance by consecration, agreeable to his law, which he has given, that he may tithe his people, to prepare them against the day of vengeance and burning, should have their names enrolled with the people of God.

dc-86.summary: The revelation explains the parable of the wheat and the tares. The field is the world, and the apostles were the sowers. After the apostles died, the apostate power called Babylon sowed tares that choked the wheat and drove the church into the wilderness. In the last days the blade is springing up again, but it is still tender. Angels are ready to reap, but the Lord tells them to wait so the wheat is not destroyed. At harvest the wheat will be gathered first, and then the tares will be bound and burned. It tells priesthood holders that they are lawful heirs through the lineage of their fathers. If they continue in the Lord’s goodness, they will be a light to the Gentiles and a savior to Israel.
dc-86.setting: On 6 December 1832, Joseph Smith was at Kirtland, Ohio, working on his revision of the Bible. His journal says he received a revelation that day explaining the parable of the wheat and the tares in Matthew 13. Sidney Rigdon wrote it down. It is not clear whether Joseph was then reviewing the New Testament or working on the Old Testament.

verse.text: Therefore, let the wheat and the tares grow together until the harvest is fully ripe; then ye shall first gather out the wheat from among the tares, and after the gathering of the wheat, behold and lo, the tares are bound in bundles, and the field remaineth to be burned.

dc-87.summary: The revelation speaks of wars that will begin with the rebellion of South Carolina. It says the Southern States will be divided against the Northern States. The South will call on Great Britain, and other nations will be drawn in until war is poured out on all nations. It says slaves will rise against their masters. It says the remnants left in the land will vex the Gentiles. Famine, plague, earthquake, and lightning will follow until there is a full end of all nations. It closes by telling the Saints to stand in holy places and not be moved until the day of the Lord.
dc-87.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation on 25 December 1832 at or near Kirtland, Ohio. That autumn South Carolina had declared federal tariffs void and threatened to leave the Union. A nearby newspaper, the Painesville Telegraph, had just reported the crisis along with cholera and plague abroad. Frederick G. Williams recorded the revelation. It was left out of the 1835 and 1844 Doctrine and Covenants and first printed in England in 1851.

verse.text: Wherefore, stand ye in holy places, and be not moved, until the day of the Lord come; for behold, it cometh quickly, saith the Lord. Amen.

dc-87.relatedNote: D&C 87 foretells war beginning with the rebellion of South Carolina. The Civil War began there in 1861.

dc-88.summary: The revelation tells the assembled elders their prayers were heard and promises “another Comforter”. It names the light of Christ as the power in the sun, moon, stars, and earth. That light gives life to all things and is the law that governs them. The earth will be sanctified for celestial beings, and each person receives the glory whose law he can abide. A parable of a lord visiting twelve servants, each in his hour, pictures God visiting his kingdoms. The elders must call a solemn assembly, sanctify themselves, teach one another, and seek learning “by study and also by faith”. Seven angels then sound trumpets over the Second Coming, the resurrections, and Michael’s final battle with the devil. The elders must build a house of God, and the closing verses set rules for the school of the prophets.
dc-88.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at a conference of high priests in Kirtland, Ohio, on 27–28 December 1832. The elders had prayed, one by one, to learn God’s will about building Zion. His scribe wrote it down, and the original manuscript is lost. On 11 January 1833 Joseph sent a copy to William W. Phelps in Missouri and called it an “olive leaf”. Verses 127–137 come from a separate revelation of 3 January 1833 on the school of the prophets, later printed with this one.

verse.text: And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.

dc-89.summary: The opening verses address the high priests in Kirtland, the church, and the Saints in Zion. They call the revelation a word of wisdom, given “not by commandment or constraint”. The voice says it warns against the designs of “conspiring men” in the last days. Wine and strong drink are not good, except homemade grape wine for the sacrament. Strong drink is for washing the body, and tobacco is for bruises and sick cattle; “hot drinks” are not for the body. Herbs, fruit, and grain are ordained for human use, and meat is to be used sparingly. Those who keep these sayings and obey are promised health, wisdom, and strength to run without weariness. The destroying angel will pass them by, as it passed ancient Israel.
dc-89.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 27 February 1833. No record from the time describes the occasion. Later accounts tie it to the school of the prophets, which met at Newel K. Whitney’s store. Brigham Young, who was not present, later said tobacco use there troubled Emma Smith and others, so Joseph asked the Lord. Temperance societies were active across America and in Kirtland at the time.

verse.text: Given for a principle with promise, adapted to the capacity of the weak and the weakest of all saints, who are or can be called saints.

dc-90.summary: The revelation forgives Joseph Smith and confirms his keys, through which “the oracles” go to the church. Sidney Rigdon and Frederick G. Williams are forgiven and made equal with Joseph in holding these keys. The three are to finish translating the prophets, then preside over the church and school, study, and learn languages. Joseph Smith Sr. and Sidney Rigdon stay where they live, Williams needs a home, and the bishop must find an agent to clear debts. Vienna Jaques is to receive money for her journey and an inheritance in Zion. The Lord is displeased with William E. McLellin and Sidney Gilbert, and the bishop and others must repent. Zion will be chastened, yet not removed from her place.
dc-90.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 8 March 1833. Jesse Gause, one of his counselors, had been excommunicated in December 1832. Frederick G. Williams was called in January 1833 to take his place. The revelation advanced the presidency of the high priesthood, and the counselors were ordained on 18 March. Leaders in Kirtland and Missouri were also in tension over Zion at the time.

verse.text: And again, verily I say unto thy brethren, Sidney Rigdon and Frederick G. Williams, their sins are forgiven them also, and they are accounted as equal with thee in holding the keys of this last kingdom;

dc-91.summary: The revelation answers a question about the Apocrypha. It says many things in those books are true and mostly translated correctly. It also says many things in them are not true but were added by human hands. The Apocrypha does not need to be translated. Whoever reads it should read with understanding, because “the Spirit manifesteth truth”. A reader enlightened by the Spirit will benefit, and one who is not will not.
dc-91.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 9 March 1833. He was revising the Bible and had finished the New Testament in February. He had reached the Apocrypha, books outside the Hebrew canon that some Bibles then included. He asked the Lord whether to revise those books too. Some Bible societies had recently stopped printing Bibles that contained them.

verse.text: Therefore, whoso readeth it, let him understand, for the Spirit manifesteth truth;

dc-92.summary: The revelation is addressed to the united order, also called the United Firm. It tells the members to receive Frederick G. Williams into the order. It adds that what is said to one is said to all. Then it speaks to Williams himself. He is to be “a lively member” of the order. If he keeps all former commandments, he will be blessed forever.
dc-92.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 15 March 1833. A week earlier, Frederick G. Williams had been named to the presidency with Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon. He had worked for the United Firm as a paid assistant scribe since January. The firm managed the church’s printing, stores, and properties in Kirtland and Missouri.

verse.text: And again, I say unto you my servant Frederick G. Williams, you shall be a lively member in this order; and inasmuch as you are faithful in keeping all former commandments you shall be blessed forever. Amen.

dc-93.summary: The revelation promises that those who forsake sin and obey will see Christ’s face and know that he is. It then quotes a record of John, who saw that Christ “received not of the fulness at first”. Christ continued “from grace to grace” until he received a fulness of the Father’s glory. Those who keep the commandments may also receive grace for grace and come to the Father’s fulness. The revelation says people were with God in the beginning, and that intelligence was not created. It defines truth as knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be, and calls God’s glory “light and truth”. Williams and Rigdon are rebuked for not teaching their children, and Joseph Smith and Whitney must set their families in order. Rigdon is to go on his journey and preach, and Joseph and Williams are to make haste also. All are to hasten the translation and study history and law.
dc-93.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 May 1833, and few sources describe its background. Part of it is addressed to Frederick G. Williams, Sidney Rigdon, and Newel K. Whitney. Whitney’s note on his copy called it a reprimand about their families, though most of the text concerns the Father and the Son. Its opening echoes John 1, but the JSP judges it separate from the New Testament revision finished in February 1833.

verse.text: And he received not of the fulness at first, but continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness;

dc-94.summary: The revelation commands the Saints to lay out Kirtland as the “city of the stake of Zion,” starting from the Lord’s house. The work must follow the pattern already given. The first lot south is for a house for the presidency, fifty-five by sixty-five feet, with lower and higher courts. It must be kept clean, or the Lord’s glory and presence will not be there. The second lot south is for a house of the same size for printing the scripture translation. Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Jared Carter receive lots and are named a committee to build the houses. The two houses are not to be built until a later commandment.
dc-94.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 2 August 1833. Earlier editions dated it 6 May 1833, an error corrected in the 2013 edition. That spring the church had bought Peter French’s farm, where the Lord’s house would stand at the center of the city plat. In the same weeks the presidency drafted plans for Kirtland and for Zion in Missouri. Kirtland leaders did not yet know that a mob in Independence had destroyed the church’s press in July.

verse.text: And ye shall not suffer any unclean thing to come in unto it; and my glory shall be there, and my presence shall be there.

dc-95.summary: The revelation opens by saying the Lord chastens those he loves to prepare their deliverance. It rebukes them for a “very grievous sin”: neglecting the command to build the house meant to prepare his apostles. Many have been called, but few chosen, and those not chosen walk “in darkness at noon-day”. The voice says the chosen will be endowed with power from on high in this house. They must tarry, as the apostles did at Jerusalem. It also names contention in the school of the prophets as grievous. The house is to be built not after the world’s manner but by a pattern shown to three men. It will measure fifty-five by sixty-five feet, with a lower court for worship and a higher court for the apostles’ school.
dc-95.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 1 June 1833. Revelations in December 1832 and January 1833 had commanded a house of the Lord and a school. In May a conference named Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Jared Carter to raise funds for it. Nearly a month later, no one had begun to build. A council then appointed Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams to plan the inner court, and work began by 7 June.

verse.text: Yea, verily I say unto you, I gave unto you a commandment that you should build a house, in the which house I design to endow those whom I have chosen with power from on high;

dc-96.summary: The revelation says this stake, set “for the strength of Zion,” must be made strong. Newel K. Whitney is to take charge of the place where the Lord’s house will be built. The land is to be divided into lots for those seeking inheritances, as the council decides. A portion is to serve the order’s purpose of bringing forth the Lord’s word. The voice calls the spread of that word “most expedient,” to subdue people’s hearts. John Johnson’s offering is accepted, and he is promised eternal life if he keeps the commandments. He is called a descendant of Joseph and is to join the order. He is to remove the debts on “the house named among you” so that he may live there.
dc-96.setting: High priests met on 4 June 1833 in the translating room of Newel K. Whitney’s store in Kirtland, Ohio. The church had recently bought the 103-acre farm of Peter French. The council could not agree on who should manage it, so they agreed to ask the Lord. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation during the meeting. That same day, the council put Whitney in charge of the farm and admitted John Johnson to the United Firm.

verse.text: For behold, verily I say unto you, this is the most expedient in me, that my word should go forth unto the children of men, for the purpose of subduing the hearts of the children of men for your good. Even so. Amen.

dc-97.summary: The revelation speaks to Joseph Smith about the Saints in Zion, many of whom are humble and seeking wisdom. It approves the school in Zion and Parley P. Pratt as its leader, as long as he abides in the Lord. Others in the school must be chastened, but the honest and contrite who keep their covenants by sacrifice are accepted. It then commands that a house be built in Zion, quickly, by the tithing of the people. The house is for thanksgiving and for instructing those called to the ministry. If it is kept undefiled, the Lord’s glory and presence will be there, and the pure in heart will see God. The revelation defines Zion as “the pure in heart.” Zion will escape coming judgments if she obeys, but will suffer if she does not.
dc-97.setting: Church members in Jackson County, Missouri, had formed a school of the prophets in the summer of 1833. Parley P. Pratt taught a class of about sixty men there each week. In early July, Oliver Cowdery and the school wrote to Joseph Smith in Kirtland, asking him to inquire about the school. Joseph dictated this revelation on 2 August and sent it to Missouri in a letter of 6 August. He did not yet know that a mob had attacked the Saints in Independence in late July.

verse.text: Therefore, verily, thus saith the Lord, let Zion rejoice, for this is Zion—THE PURE IN HEART; therefore, let Zion rejoice, while all the wicked shall mourn.

dc-98.summary: The revelation tells the Saints not to fear, to give thanks, and to wait on the Lord. It promises that their afflictions will work together for their good. It says the constitutional law that protects freedom is justified, and that honest and wise leaders should be sought. It calls the Saints to renounce war and proclaim peace. It rebukes many in the Kirtland church for pride and covetousness. Then it gives a law for enduring attacks: bear the first, second, and third offense patiently. After warning an enemy, the injured may be justified in defending themselves. It also gives an ancient pattern of offering peace three times before war, It commands forgiveness of a repentant enemy every time. An unrepentant enemy is forgiven three times, and the fourth offense is brought before the Lord.
dc-98.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 August 1833. Two weeks earlier, a mob in Independence, Missouri, had destroyed the Church printing office and tarred and feathered Bishop Edward Partridge and Charles Allen. On 23 July, Church leaders there agreed under pressure to leave Jackson County. The official heading says Joseph could have known the seriousness of events only by revelation. The Joseph Smith Papers notes the text never names Jackson County and may also reflect rising opposition in Kirtland. It was copied into a letter to Missouri the same day.

verse.text: Therefore, renounce war and proclaim peace, and seek diligently to turn the hearts of the children to their fathers, and the hearts of the fathers to the children;

dc-99.summary: The revelation calls John Murdock to preach in the eastern countries. He is to go from house to house, village to village, and city to city, amid persecution. Those who receive him receive the Lord, and he will speak with the power of the Spirit. Those who reject him will be rejected, and he is to cleanse his feet as a testimony against them. He is not to leave until his children are provided for and sent kindly to the bishop in Zion. After a few years he may go to Zion for his inheritance, if he wishes. Otherwise he is to keep preaching until he is taken.
dc-99.setting: John Murdock joined the Church in Ohio in November 1830 and gave himself to preaching. His wife, Julia Clapp, died in April 1831 after giving birth to twins. Joseph and Emma Smith adopted the twins, and other families cared for his older children. One twin died in March 1832 after the mob attack on the Johnson home in Hiram. Murdock returned to Ohio sick that summer. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation for him at Hiram on 29 August 1832.

verse.text: And now, verily I say unto you, that it is not expedient that you should go until your children are provided for, and sent up kindly unto the bishop of Zion.

dc-100.summary: The revelation tells Sidney Rigdon and Joseph Smith that their families are well and in the Lord’s hands. It says the Lord has many people in this region, and an effectual door will open. They are to speak what is put into their hearts, in solemnity and meekness. The Holy Ghost will bear record of what they say. Sidney is called as a spokesman for Joseph, and Joseph is to be a revelator to Sidney. It promises that Zion will be redeemed, though chastened for a season. Orson Hyde and John Gould are in the Lord’s hands. All things will work together for good to the upright.
dc-100.setting: Freeman and Huldah Nickerson of Perrysburg, New York, came to Kirtland in September 1833. They asked Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to preach to their family in New York and Upper Canada. Joseph and Sidney left Kirtland with them on 5 October. They reached the Nickerson home in Perrysburg on 12 October, worried about the families they had left. This revelation was recorded there that day. The two then went on to preach and baptize in Upper Canada.

verse.text: For it shall be given you in the very hour, yea, in the very moment, what ye shall say.

dc-101.summary: The revelation says the Lord allowed the affliction because of the Saints’ transgressions, naming contention, envy, and covetous desires. Yet it promises compassion and says the Lord will not cast them off. Zion will not be moved, and the pure in heart will return to build its waste places. It describes the day of the Lord’s coming, when enmity ends and all things are revealed. A parable tells of a nobleman’s servants who neglected to build a watchtower and lost the vineyard. The lord then sends a servant to gather the strength of his house and redeem it. The churches are to keep gathering, buy land in Jackson County, and not sell their claims there. The Saints are to petition the judge, the governor, and the president, under a Constitution the text says God established. Sidney Gilbert is told not to sell the storehouse.
dc-101.setting: In late October and early November 1833, armed residents drove the Latter-day Saints out of Jackson County, Missouri. Two attackers died in a clash on 4 November, and a militia then disarmed the Saints. Most refugees crossed into Clay County, losing homes, goods, livestock, and crops. In Kirtland, Joseph Smith heard reports from Orson Hyde and John Gould and letters from Edward Partridge and others. Joseph dictated this revelation on 16–17 December 1833. The earliest known copy is undated; later copies give these dates.

verse.text: Therefore, let your hearts be comforted concerning Zion; for all flesh is in mine hands; be still and know that I am God.

dc-101.relatedNote: In D&C 101:80 the Lord says he established the Constitution of this land.

dc-102.summary: These are minutes, not a revelation in the Lord’s voice. They record the organizing of a high council of twelve high priests, with one or three presidents. Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick Williams are acknowledged as presidents. Twelve councilors are chosen, including Joseph Smith’s father, Martin Harris, and Oliver Cowdery. The minutes set a quorum of seven, a way to fill vacancies, and an order for speaking by drawn numbers. Half the council stands for the accused, and the president decides with the council’s vote or a rehearing. Traveling high priests may form councils abroad, with appeal to the high council at the First Presidency’s seat.
dc-102.setting: On 17 February 1834, twenty-four high priests met at Joseph Smith’s house in Kirtland, Ohio. They organized a standing high council to settle serious disputes the Church or a bishop’s council could not resolve. Clerk Orson Hyde noted that some errors were likely made, and the meeting asked Joseph to correct them. Joseph revised the minutes the next day. On 19 February the council accepted them unanimously as its form and constitution. Verses 30–32, about the Twelve Apostles, were added in 1835.

verse.text: The accused, in all cases, has a right to one-half of the council, to prevent insult or injustice.

dc-103.summary: The revelation tells the Lord’s “friends” how to act for their scattered brethren in Zion. It says the Saints were chastened because they did not fully obey. If they now hearken, they will begin to prevail. If not, the world will prevail against them. The scattered will return and build up Zion, but only if they do not pollute their inheritances. Zion’s redemption must come by power, led by a man like Moses. Joseph Smith is named as the servant in the earlier parable of the vineyard. He is to gather the young and middle-aged men to Zion. Pairs of recruiters are sent out to seek five hundred men, and no fewer than one hundred.
dc-103.setting: Two Missouri leaders, Parley Pratt and Lyman Wight, arrived in Kirtland on 24 February 1834. They reported to the Kirtland high council on the exiled Saints, most of them in Clay County. They asked how Zion would be redeemed. At that meeting Joseph Smith offered to lead an expedition, and thirty or forty others volunteered. Joseph dictated this revelation the same day, but records do not show whether before, during, or after the meeting.

verse.text: Behold, I say unto you, the redemption of Zion must needs come by power;

routes.title: Recruiting mission to western New York
Camp of Israel: the Michigan group

dc-104.summary: The revelation addresses the order the Lord commanded to be organized. It says some members broke the covenant through covetousness and feigned words, and are cursed. Members are to be organized and each given a stewardship to account for. It says the earth is the Lord’s, there is enough and to spare, and the poor are to be exalted. It assigns Kirtland properties to Sidney Rigdon, Martin Harris, Frederick Williams, Oliver Cowdery, John Johnson, Newel Whitney, and Joseph Smith. The Kirtland and Missouri branches are separated. Two treasuries are created, one for the sacred writings and one for stewardship income. Members are to pay their debts and write to New York, and may pledge their properties this once.
dc-104.setting: The United Firm was formed in 1832 to run the Church’s stores and printing. By 1834 it was deep in debt, and the Missouri store and press had been lost to mob violence. Some members were accused of treating firm property as their own. On 10 April 1834 the Kirtland members voted to dissolve the firm. This revelation, given at or near Kirtland on 23 April, instead reorganized it. The 1835 edition later used substitute names and called it the “United Order.”

verse.text: And if the properties are mine, then ye are stewards; otherwise ye are no stewards.

dc-105.summary: The revelation, addressed to those gathered, says Zion could have been redeemed already but for the church’s transgressions. It names disobedience, failure to share with the poor, and lack of union, mainly among the churches abroad. It says the elders must wait “for a little season” and first be “endowed with power from on high”. That endowment is to come in the house being built in Kirtland. It says the Lord will fight Zion’s battles and accepts the offering of those who came. Those who can stay in the region should stay; those with families in the east are to follow Joseph’s direction. The Saints are to buy land in Jackson County and nearby counties, gather quietly, and not boast. It closes by telling them to “sue for peace” with all people.
dc-105.setting: Joseph Smith led an armed expedition, later called Zion’s Camp, from Ohio to Missouri in May and June 1834. It aimed to help Saints driven from Jackson County regain their lands. Governor Daniel Dunklin did not call out the militia to escort them, and a Clay County delegation warned of violence. On 22 June 1834, at a campsite about four miles north of Fishing River, Joseph dictated this revelation. Soon after, the camp disbanded, and cholera struck many members.

verse.text: That they themselves may be prepared, and that my people may be taught more perfectly, and have experience, and know more perfectly concerning their duty, and the things which I require at their hands.

routes.title: Camp of Israel: the Michigan group

dc-106.summary: The revelation calls Warren A. Cowdery to be ordained a presiding high priest over the church in Freedom and nearby areas. He is to preach and warn people there and in adjoining counties. He is to give his whole time to the calling, and the text says “the laborer is worthy of his hire”. It warns that the Lord’s coming will overtake the world “as a thief in the night”. Those who are “children of light” need not be caught off guard. It says heaven rejoiced when Warren turned from “the crafts of men”. Despite “the vanity of his heart,” he will be lifted up if he humbles himself. If he stays a faithful witness, a crown is prepared for him.
dc-106.setting: Warren A. Cowdery, an older brother of Oliver Cowdery, lived in Freedom, New York. He had corresponded with Oliver in Kirtland and was not yet a member in spring 1834. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation for him at Kirtland on 25 November 1834. Freedom served as a gathering point for several branches in western New York.

verse.text: Therefore, blessed is my servant Warren, for I will have mercy on him; and, notwithstanding the vanity of his heart, I will lift him up inasmuch as he will humble himself before me.

dc-107.summary: The instruction says the church has two priesthoods, the Melchizedek and the Aaronic. It explains their names and gives each priesthood its keys and duties. It sets out presiding quorums: the Presidency of the Church, the Twelve, and the Seventy. Their decisions must be unanimous and made in righteousness, with appeal possible when a decision is unrighteous. It traces a patriarchal order from Adam through Noah and describes Adam’s last blessing at Adam-ondi-Ahman. Then it details bishops and church councils, including a council that can try the church president. It gives quorum sizes and presidents for deacons, teachers, priests, elders, and the Seventy. It ends: “let every man learn his duty” and act “in all diligence”.
dc-107.setting: In February and March 1835, the church organized the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and the first Seventy. The Twelve were preparing to leave Kirtland on 4 May 1835 for conferences in the eastern states. Joseph Smith gave them this instruction on priesthood sometime between about 1 March and 4 May. Most of verses 60–100 draws on a revelation he dictated in November 1831. It was printed as “On Priesthood” in the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants.

verse.text: Wherefore, now let every man learn his duty, and to act in the office in which he is appointed, in all diligence.

dc-108.summary: The revelation tells Lyman that his sins are forgiven because he came that morning to seek counsel. It tells him to let his soul rest about his spiritual standing and to resist the Lord’s voice no more. He should keep his vows more carefully and will be greatly blessed. He is to wait for the solemn assembly. Then he will be remembered with the first elders and ordained with them. From that time he will have right to preach wherever he is sent. He is to strengthen his brethren in conversation, prayer, exhortation, and action. The Lord promises to be with him to bless and deliver him.
dc-108.setting: Lyman Sherman joined the church in New York in 1832 and moved to Kirtland in 1833. He marched with Zion’s Camp and was called in February 1835 as one of seven presidents of the Seventy. On 26 December 1835 he visited Joseph Smith, who was studying Hebrew. Sherman said he had been promised a revelation that would make known his duty. Joseph dictated this response that day, likely with Frederick G. Williams as scribe.

verse.text: Therefore, let your soul be at rest concerning your spiritual standing, and resist no more my voice.

dc-109.summary: The prayer thanks God and asks him to accept the house the Saints built through poverty and tribulation. It repeats the earlier command to build a house of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, and order. It asks that God’s glory and presence rest there and that all who enter feel his power. It asks that servants go out armed with power and that enemies and lying reports fail. It pleads for the Saints driven from Jackson County, Missouri. It asks mercy for nations and rulers, the Constitution’s preservation, and the redemption of Jerusalem and scattered Israel. It remembers Joseph Smith, his family, the church presidents, and the whole church. It closes by asking God to accept the dedication, with the cry “Hosanna to God and the Lamb!”
dc-109.setting: Latter-day Saints in Kirtland, Ohio, had worked since 1833 to build the House of the Lord. On 26 March 1836, Joseph Smith met with Oliver Cowdery, Sidney Rigdon, and scribes to prepare the dedicatory prayer. The official heading says the prayer was given to them by revelation. It was printed overnight so Joseph could read it. On 27 March 1836, he read it to about 1,000 people, who accepted it by vote.

verse.text: And that all people who shall enter upon the threshold of the Lord's house may feel thy power, and feel constrained to acknowledge that thou hast sanctified it, and that it is thy house, a place of thy holiness.

dc-110.summary: The account says the veil was taken from the minds of Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. They report seeing the Lord standing on the pulpit, with eyes like fire and a voice like rushing waters. He declares their sins forgiven and says he has accepted the house. He promises to appear there if his people keep it holy, and says its fame will spread. Then Moses appears and commits the keys of gathering Israel and leading the ten tribes. Elias commits the dispensation of the gospel of Abraham. Elijah appears last, saying the time Malachi spoke of has fully come. He commits keys tied to turning the hearts of fathers and children to each other.
dc-110.setting: One week after the dedication, on Easter Sunday, 3 April 1836, the Saints met in the Kirtland temple. After the sacrament, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery withdrew behind lowered veils at the pulpit to pray in silence. Warren A. Cowdery recorded their account in Joseph’s journal in the third person. Willard Richards later recast it in the first person, and it entered the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.

verse.text: For behold, I have accepted this house, and my name shall be here; and I will manifest myself to my people in mercy in this house.

dc-111.summary: The revelation says the Lord is “not displeased” with the journey, despite their “follies”. It says there is much treasure in Salem for Zion, and people to gather in due time. It tells them to form acquaintances with men in the city. It promises the city and its gold and silver will be theirs in due time. It tells them not to worry about their debts or about Zion. They should stay in the area, and the Spirit’s peace will show where. They are to inquire about the city’s early inhabitants and founders. It ends with counsel to be “wise as serpents” and a promise to “order all things for your good”.
dc-111.setting: The church carried heavy debts from building the Kirtland temple and buying land in Ohio and Missouri. In late July 1836, Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Oliver Cowdery, and Sidney Rigdon traveled east, staying in Salem, Massachusetts, from 5 August. The official heading says they had heard that a large sum of money might be available there. No contemporary record states their reasons, and no money came of the trip. The revelation is dated 6 August 1836.

verse.text: Therefore, be ye as wise as serpents and yet without sin; and I will order all things for your good, as fast as ye are able to receive them. Amen.

dc-112.summary: The revelation tells Thomas B. Marsh that his prayers and alms for the Twelve are heard. It says some things in his heart displeased the Lord, but his sins are forgiven because he humbled himself. He is to bear record to Gentiles and Jews and keep his home in Zion. It tells him to be humble, pray for the Twelve, and admonish them sharply. The Lord says he will heal them if they do not harden their hearts. The Twelve are told not to rebel against Joseph, who keeps the keys until the Lord comes. Marsh holds the keys of the kingdom for the Twelve abroad, under the First Presidency. It warns that judgment will begin at the Lord’s house and calls the Twelve to purify their hearts.
dc-112.setting: In 1837, many church members in Kirtland, including some apostles, turned against Joseph Smith’s leadership. Thomas B. Marsh, president of the Quorum of the Twelve, came from Far West, Missouri, in July to reconcile the quorum. He had also been troubled that some apostles planned missions abroad without consulting him. In June, Heber C. Kimball and Orson Hyde had left to preach in England. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation to Marsh at Kirtland on 23 July 1837.

verse.text: Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.

dc-113.summary: The section is a set of questions and answers on Isaiah. It says the Stem of Jesse in Isaiah 11 is Christ. The rod is a servant in Christ’s hands, descended from Jesse and from Ephraim. The root of Jesse is a descendant of Jesse and Joseph who holds priesthood and keys for the gathering. Elias Higbee then asks about Isaiah 52’s command, “Put on thy strength, O Zion”. The answer says this means putting on priesthood authority, which Zion has a right to by lineage. Zion loosing the bands from her neck means scattered Israel returning to the Lord.
dc-113.setting: Joseph Smith arrived at Far West, Missouri, in mid-March 1838 after leaving Kirtland. Between about 16 and 29 March, he answered questions about Isaiah 11 and Isaiah 52. An unnamed person asked the first three; Elias Higbee, a Caldwell County judge and high councilor, asked the others. George W. Robinson later copied both sets into Joseph’s Scriptory Book. They were first combined and published in 1853.

verse.text: He had reference to those whom God should call in the last days, who should hold the power of priesthood to bring again Zion, and the redemption of Israel; and to put on her strength is to put on the authority of the priesthood, which she, Zion, has a right to by lineage; also to return to that power which she had lost.

routes.title: Joseph Smith moves from Kirtland to Far West

dc-114.summary: The revelation tells David W. Patten to settle his business as soon as he can. He is to dispose of his merchandise. This will free him to go on a mission the next spring. He will go with others, twelve including himself, to testify to all the world. The revelation then says some among them deny the Lord’s name. Others will be planted in their place and receive their “bishopric”.
dc-114.setting: David W. Patten, a member of the Twelve, was living in Far West, Missouri, by 1837. In April 1838, he reported he could not support several apostles who had turned against Joseph Smith. On 11 April 1838, Joseph dictated this revelation for Patten at Far West. A July 1838 revelation later set the Twelve’s mission abroad for 1839. Patten was killed in October 1838, before that mission began.

verse.text: For verily thus saith the Lord, that inasmuch as there are those among you who deny my name, others shall be planted in their stead and receive their bishopric. Amen.

dc-115.summary: The revelation addresses the First Presidency, Bishop Edward Partridge, the high council in Zion, and all members. It gives the Church its name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It calls the Saints to “arise and shine forth” as a standard for the nations. Gathering to Zion and her stakes is to be a defense and a refuge. Far West is declared holy, and a house of worship is to be built there. Work is to begin on 4 July, following a pattern shown to the presidency. Joseph, Sidney Rigdon, and Hyrum Smith must not go further into debt to build it. Far West is to grow quickly, and Joseph will name other stakes nearby.
dc-115.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 26 April 1838. He had moved there from Kirtland in March, after dissent divided the Church in Ohio. Thousands of Saints lived in and around Far West, and hundreds more were on the way. Members had begun digging a temple foundation in 1837, but leaders paused the work until the Lord’s will was known. George W. Robinson copied the revelation into Joseph’s journal.

verse.text: For thus shall my church be called in the last days, even The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

routes.title: Joseph Smith moves from Kirtland to Far West

dc-116.summary: This section is one sentence from Joseph Smith’s journal, not a full revelation. It reports that the Lord named Spring Hill “Adam-ondi-Ahman”. It then gives the reason for the name. The place is where Adam “shall come to visit his people”. It links the site to the Ancient of Days in the prophet Daniel’s vision.
dc-116.setting: In mid-May 1838, Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and others traveled north from Far West into Daviess County, Missouri. On 19 May they went from their camp to Lyman Wight’s ferry on the Grand River to choose land for a new city. Wight had settled near a rise called Spring Hill and urged others to settle there. Joseph’s journal, kept by George W. Robinson, records the new name for the site. The official heading gives the date more loosely as May or June 1838.

verse.text: Spring Hill is named by the Lord Adam-ondi-Ahman, because, said he, it is the place where Adam shall come to visit his people, or the Ancient of Days shall sit, as spoken of by Daniel the prophet.

dc-117.summary: The revelation tells William Marks and Bishop Whitney to settle their business and leave Kirtland before winter. It warns that delay will not go well for them. It asks them to repent of covetous desires and asks, “what is property unto me?” The Kirtland properties may go to pay debts. The voice points to Adam-ondi-Ahman as land with room enough. Marks is to preside at Far West, and Whitney is to be a bishop at Adam-ondi-Ahman after turning from his “littleness of soul”. Oliver Granger is to work for the First Presidency’s redemption, and his name will be held in sacred remembrance. He is to come to Zion and in time become a merchant for the Lord’s people. Last, the Kirtland members are told to keep the Lord’s house holy.
dc-117.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. It was one of five he dictated that Sunday about Church leaders and finances. William Marks presided over the Church in Kirtland, Ohio, and handled debts for Joseph and Sidney Rigdon. Newel K. Whitney was the Kirtland bishop. Oliver Granger, a Church agent, had probably just arrived from Kirtland with news.

verse.text: Therefore, let him contend earnestly for the redemption of the First Presidency of my Church, saith the Lord; and when he falls he shall rise again, for his sacrifice shall be more sacred unto me than his increase, saith the Lord.

dc-118.summary: The revelation calls for a conference to organize the Twelve and fill the places of the fallen. It tells Thomas to stay in Zion for a time to publish the word. The other apostles are to keep preaching with humility and patience. If they do, the Lord promises to provide for their families. Next spring they are to cross “the great waters” to preach. They are to leave from the Far West temple site on 26 April 1839. John Taylor, John Page, Wilford Woodruff, and Willard Richards are named to fill the vacancies.
dc-118.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. Leaders had prayed to know the Lord’s will about the Twelve. Dissent in 1837 and 1838 had cost the quorum four members. Luke Johnson, John Boynton, and Lyman Johnson were cut off, and William McLellin was found in transgression. Thomas Marsh, the quorum president, was the only apostle at the meeting.

verse.text: Let them take leave of my saints in the city of Far West, on the twenty-sixth day of April next, on the building-spot of my house, saith the Lord.

dc-119.summary: The revelation asks the Saints to give all their surplus property to the bishop in Zion. The funds are for the temple, the foundation of Zion, the priesthood, and the Presidency’s debts. This first gift is called “the beginning of the tithing”. After that, members are to pay one-tenth of their interest each year. The revelation calls this “a standing law” forever. Those who gather to Zion must keep it, or they will not be worthy to stay. If the people do not keep it, the land will not be Zion to them. The law is to be an example for all the stakes.
dc-119.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. He had asked how much of the Saints’ property the Lord required as tithing. At that time “tithing” meant any donation to Church funds, not a set tenth. The Church carried heavy debt from the Kirtland Temple, failed Ohio ventures, and the Panic of 1837. The Saints also needed money to build up their Missouri settlements.

verse.text: And after that, those who have thus been tithed shall pay one-tenth of all their interest annually; and this shall be a standing law unto them forever, for my holy priesthood, saith the Lord.

dc-120.summary: This short revelation follows directly from the law of tithing in section 119. It says the time has come to decide how tithed property is used. A council is to make those decisions. The council includes the First Presidency, the bishop and his counselors, and the high council. The revelation adds that the Lord’s “own voice” will guide them.
dc-120.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. It followed section 119 on the same day and answered how tithed property should be used. In 1837 two Missouri leaders had made money decisions without the bishop or high council. That had caused resentment among high council members. The council named here met as directed on 26 July 1838.

verse.text: Verily, thus saith the Lord, the time is now come, that it shall be disposed of by a council, composed of the First Presidency of my Church, and of the bishop and his council, and by my high council; and by mine own voice unto them, saith the Lord. Even so. Amen.

dc-121.summary: The section opens with a prayer: “O God, where art thou?” Joseph asks how long the Saints must suffer and pleads for God to act. A reply then speaks to him as “my son” and promises peace. His trial will be “but a small moment,” and his friends still stand by him. The text warns those who falsely accuse the Saints, drive them, and kill them. It promises knowledge by the Holy Ghost that has not been revealed before. It says many are called but few chosen, because they seek worldly honors. Priesthood power, it says, rests only on persuasion, patience, gentleness, meekness, kindness, and unfeigned love.
dc-121.setting: Joseph Smith wrote this from the jail at Liberty, Clay County, Missouri, in March 1839. He, Hyrum Smith, Lyman Wight, Caleb Baldwin, and Alexander McRae had been held there since 1 December 1838. They awaited trial on charges from the 1838 conflict in Missouri. Governor Lilburn Boggs had ordered the Saints out of the state, and most had fled to Illinois. Appeals to officials had brought no relief. The section joins passages from two letters to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, dated 20 March and about 22 March.

verse.text: No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned;

routes.title: Joseph Smith taken to Liberty Jail

dc-122.summary: The voice tells Joseph that the ends of the earth will ask about his name. Fools will mock him, but the pure in heart will seek his counsel. Traitors will not turn his people against him. It then lists trials: false accusation, being torn from family, prison, and a sentence of death. It pictures his six-year-old son clinging to him and asking why he cannot stay. All these things, it says, “shall give thee experience” and be for his good. It says the Son of Man has descended below them all. Joseph should hold on, for his days are known and God will be with him.
dc-122.setting: Joseph Smith was a prisoner in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, when this text was written. It comes from a letter to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church dated about 22 March 1839. Joseph likely dictated it, and fellow prisoner Alexander McRae wrote it out. In the letter the voice shifts from the prisoners to words addressed to Joseph as “my son”. By then Joseph had been held in Liberty for nearly four months.

verse.text: The Son of Man hath descended below them all. Art thou greater than he?

routes.title: Joseph Smith taken to Liberty Jail

dc-123.summary: The letter suggests the Saints gather the facts of their suffering in Missouri. They should record property losses and injuries to character and person. They should list the names of those who oppressed them. A committee might take statements and affidavits and collect libelous publications. The goal is to publish the record and present it to the heads of government. The letter calls this an “imperative duty” to God, to families, to widows and orphans, and to the rising generation. Many people of all faiths, it says, miss the truth only because they do not know where to find it. It ends by urging the Saints to do all they can, then stand still and trust God.
dc-123.setting: Joseph Smith wrote this in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, in an undated letter of about 22 March 1839. His fellow prisoners also signed it. The letter went to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, by way of Quincy, Illinois, where many Saints had fled. The Saints had lost homes, land, and lives in the Missouri conflict of 1838. The letter recalls the killings at Hawn’s Mill and the death of apostle David Patten.

verse.text: For there are many yet on the earth among all sects, parties, and denominations, who are blinded by the subtle craftiness of men, whereby they lie in wait to deceive, and who are only kept from the truth because they know not where to find it—

routes.title: Joseph Smith taken to Liberty Jail

dc-124.summary: The revelation accepts Joseph’s offering and calls for a proclamation to the kings and rulers of the earth. It names helpers, including Robert Thompson and John Bennett, and praises Hyrum Smith and George Miller. It commands the Saints to bring their wealth and skill and build a temple in Nauvoo. Baptisms for the dead outside the temple are accepted only for a set time. If the Saints do not build, they will be rejected as a church with their dead. The Lord accepts the offering of those hindered in Jackson County and tells the Saints to build again. A boarding house called the Nauvoo House is to be funded by stock under set rules. The revelation then counsels many individuals, calls Hyrum as patriarch, adds William Law to the First Presidency, and names the Church’s quorum leaders.
dc-124.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Nauvoo, Illinois, on 19 January 1841. The Saints had been forced out of Missouri after Governor Lilburn Boggs’s order of 27 October 1838. They settled at Commerce, Illinois, renamed it Nauvoo, and made it Church headquarters. Joseph Smith Sr., David Patten, and Edward Partridge had died since 1838. Church clerk Robert Thompson copied the revelation into the Book of the Law of the Lord.

verse.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, that when I give a commandment to any of the sons of men to do a work unto my name, and those sons of men go with all their might and with all they have to perform that work, and cease not their diligence, and their enemies come upon them and hinder them from performing that work, behold, it behooveth me to require that work no more at the hands of those sons of men, but to accept of their offerings.

dc-125.summary: The section opens with a question about the Lord’s will for the Saints in Iowa Territory. The answer sets a condition: if they will do his will, they should gather. They are to gather to places the Lord appoints through Joseph Smith. They are to build cities so they will be ready for what is coming. The revelation names a city to be built across the river from Nauvoo, called Zarahemla. People arriving from every direction may settle there. They may also take inheritances in Nashville, in Nauvoo, or in the appointed stakes.
dc-125.setting: After leaving Missouri in 1839, most Latter-day Saints settled in Hancock County, Illinois. Smaller groups lived in scattered settlements across the river in Iowa Territory. In early March 1841, Joseph Smith dictated this answer at Nauvoo to a question about those Iowa Saints. It may relate to an 11 March visit by John Smith, who led the Iowa stake, to learn the Lord’s will. The exact day is uncertain because the first copy was made later without a date.

verse.text: Verily, thus saith the Lord, I say unto you, if those who call themselves by my name and are essaying to be my saints, if they will do my will and keep my commandments concerning them, let them gather themselves together unto the places which I shall appoint unto them by my servant Joseph, and build up cities unto my name, that they may be prepared for that which is in store for a time to come.

dc-126.summary: This short revelation addresses Brigham Young as a dear and well-beloved brother. The Lord’s voice tells Brigham he no longer has to leave his family as before. It says his offering is accepted. It says the Lord has seen his labor and travel for His name. Then it gives two commands. Brigham is to send the Lord’s word abroad. He is also to take special care of his family from then on.
dc-126.setting: Brigham Young left Nauvoo in 1839 for a mission to England with other apostles. His wife, Mary Ann Angell Young, and their children faced poverty and illness while he was gone. Young, Heber Kimball, and John Taylor arrived back in Nauvoo on 1 July 1841. Eight days later, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Young’s home. Willard Richards copied it into the Book of the Law of the Lord that December.

verse.text: I therefore command you to send my word abroad, and take especial care of your family from this time, henceforth and forever. Amen.
