dc-127.summary: Joseph Smith writes to the Saints explaining why he has left home for a time. He says enemies in Missouri and Illinois pursue him without just cause. He has left his business with agents and will return when the storm passes. He says danger has been his lot all his life, yet God has always delivered him. A revelation then tells the Saints to continue the temple work with redoubled diligence. It directs that a recorder witness every baptism for the dead, so what is recorded on earth may be recorded in heaven. The records are to be kept in order in the temple. Joseph closes, unable to speak in person, and promises more letters.
dc-127.setting: In August 1842 Joseph Smith faced arrest and possible extradition to Missouri. Former Missouri governor Lilburn Boggs and John Bennett had accused him of a part in an attempt on Boggs’s life. Joseph hid with friends in and near Nauvoo and across the river in Iowa Territory. On 1 September he dictated this letter to William Clayton. It was read to the Saints in the grove near the temple site on 4 September. Baptisms for the dead had been performed since 1840, and the temple font was dedicated in November 1841.

verse.text: That in all your recordings it may be recorded in heaven; whatsoever you bind on earth, may be bound in heaven; whatsoever you loose on earth, may be loosed in heaven;

dc-128.summary: Joseph Smith resumes the subject of baptism for the dead in a second letter. He revises his earlier instruction so each ward may have its own recorder and witnesses. A general recorder will then copy these certified records into a church book. Citing Revelation 20 and Matthew 16, he says what is recorded on earth is recorded in heaven. He calls the baptismal font a likeness of the grave, placed beneath where the living meet. Quoting Paul and Malachi, he says the living and the dead cannot be made perfect without each other. He then recalls voices from heaven: Moroni at Cumorah, Michael, Peter, James, and John, and others. He calls for courage and asks the Saints to present “a book containing the records of our dead” in the temple.
dc-128.setting: A week after his first letter, Joseph Smith was still hiding from officers sent to arrest him. He dictated this second letter on 7 September 1842 at the Nauvoo home of Edward Hunter. Officers from Adams County and an agent from Missouri had come for him on 3 September. The letter was read to the Saints at the grove near the temple on 11 September. That evening the general church recorder began a new book following its instructions. It was printed in the Times and Seasons on 1 October 1842.

verse.text: I might have rendered a plainer translation to this, but it is sufficiently plain to suit my purpose as it stands. It is sufficient to know, in this case, that the earth will be smitten with a curse unless there is a welding link of some kind or other between the fathers and the children, upon some subject or other—and behold what is that subject? It is the baptism for the dead. For we without them cannot be made perfect; neither can they without us be made perfect. Neither can they nor we be made perfect without those who have died in the gospel also; for it is necessary in the ushering in of the dispensation of the fulness of times, which dispensation is now beginning to usher in, that a whole and complete and perfect union, and welding together of dispensations, and keys, and powers, and glories should take place, and be revealed from the days of Adam even to the present time. And not only this, but those things which never have been revealed from the foundation of the world, but have been kept hid from the wise and prudent, shall be revealed unto babes and sucklings in this, the dispensation of the fulness of times.

dc-129.summary: These instructions say there are two kinds of beings in heaven. Angels are resurrected and have bodies of flesh and bones, as Jesus said of himself. The spirits of just men made perfect are not resurrected but share the same glory. When a messenger claims to come from God, ask him to shake hands. An angel will do so, and you will feel his hand. A just spirit will not move, because deceiving is against heaven’s order, but he will still give his message. If the devil comes as an angel of light, you will feel nothing and can detect him. The section calls these “three grand keys” for judging any messenger.
dc-129.setting: On 9 February 1843, several visitors called at Joseph Smith’s home in Nauvoo. Parley and Orson Pratt were among them; Parley had returned to the city two days before. Joseph talked with them informally about how to tell true heavenly messengers from false ones. He had taught similar ideas in 1839, while Parley was jailed in Missouri. William Clayton and Willard Richards both recorded the remarks. Orson Pratt adapted Clayton’s version for the 1876 Doctrine and Covenants.

verse.text: If it be the devil as an angel of light, when you ask him to shake hands he will offer you his hand, and you will not feel anything; you may therefore detect him.

dc-130.summary: In separate teachings, Joseph says the Savior will appear as “a man like ourselves”. He says the same “sociality” will continue there, joined with eternal glory. He calls the idea that the Father and Son dwell in a person’s heart false. He says angels who minister to this earth belong or have belonged to it, and God’s dwelling is “a great Urim and Thummim”. He repeats a prophecy from 25 December 1832 that bloodshed before Christ’s coming will begin in South Carolina, probably over “the slave question”. He recalls a voice saying he would see the Son of Man if he lived to eighty-five. Knowledge gained in this life rises in the resurrection, and every blessing comes by obeying a law. The Father and Son have bodies of flesh and bones, but the Holy Ghost is a personage of Spirit.
dc-130.setting: On Sunday, 2 April 1843, Joseph Smith was in Ramus, also called Macedonia, Illinois. He had spent the night at the home of Benjamin and Melissa Johnson. Orson Hyde preached that morning, and Joseph later corrected parts of his sermon. Some followers of William Miller expected Christ to return the next day, and Joseph addressed that interest. William Clayton recorded the teachings, which were drawn out by questions from those present. Parts of Willard Richards’s version became section 130 in 1876.

verse.text: And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.

dc-131.summary: The section opens with three heavens or degrees within the celestial glory. To obtain the highest, a man must enter an order of the priesthood. A bracketed note explains this as the new and everlasting covenant of marriage. Without it, he may enter another degree but cannot have an increase. A note dated 17 May defines the “more sure word of prophecy”. It means knowing by revelation that one is sealed up to eternal life. The section says no one can be saved in ignorance. It ends by saying all spirit is matter, too fine to be seen now.
dc-131.setting: In mid-May 1843 Joseph Smith visited Ramus, also called Macedonia, Illinois. On 16 May he taught William Clayton and Benjamin and Melissa Johnson at the Johnson home. His subject was priesthood and the sealing of marriage. On 17 May he preached on 2 Peter 1 and spoke again that evening. Clayton recorded these teachings in his journal, and they were later combined as section 131.

verse.text: And in order to obtain the highest, a man must enter into this order of the priesthood [meaning the new and everlasting covenant of marriage];

dc-132.summary: The revelation answers Joseph’s question about how God justified Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon in having many wives and concubines. It reveals a “new and everlasting covenant,” saying covenants not sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise end at death. Marriages made only for this world end then, but marriages sealed by the one holding the keys endure toward exaltation. It says Abraham did not sin in taking Hagar and concubines because God commanded it, and David sinned only concerning Uriah’s wife. It confirms Joseph’s power to seal on earth and in heaven. Emma Smith is told to receive Joseph’s wives and cleave to him or be destroyed; if she forgives him, she will be blessed. Under the “law of the priesthood,” a man may marry more virgins with his first wife’s consent. If she rejects the law, verse 64 says she will be destroyed, and verse 65 frees him from “the law of Sarah,” her consent.
dc-132.setting: On 12 July 1843, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation to William Clayton in his Nauvoo office. The official heading says Joseph likely knew some of its principles well before 1843. Hyrum Smith urged him to write it down, hoping it would persuade Emma Smith to accept plural marriage. The Joseph Smith Papers editors count about twenty-five confidential plural sealings by then, many unknown to Emma. Emma rejected the document and later destroyed the original, but a copy by Joseph Kingsbury survived. It was first published in 1852 and added to the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.

verse.text: And verily I say unto you, that the conditions of this law are these: All covenants, contracts, bonds, obligations, oaths, vows, performances, connections, associations, or expectations, that are not made and entered into and sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise, of him who is anointed, both as well for time and for all eternity, and that too most holy, by revelation and commandment through the medium of mine anointed, whom I have appointed on the earth to hold this power (and I have appointed unto my servant Joseph to hold this power in the last days, and there is never but one on the earth at a time on whom this power and the keys of this priesthood are conferred), are of no efficacy, virtue, or force in and after the resurrection from the dead; for all contracts that are not made unto this end have an end when men are dead.

dc-133.summary: The Lord’s voice calls on the Church to hear, for he will suddenly come to his temple in judgment. It tells the Saints to prepare, sanctify themselves, and gather to Zion, leaving Babylon behind. Elders are to go to all nations, first the Gentiles and then the Jews. Gentiles are to flee to Zion and Judah to Jerusalem, but not in haste. The revelation describes the Lord’s coming: lands joined, those in the north countries returning, and the saints rising from their graves. It pictures Christ in red garments, having “trodden the wine-press alone,” while his redeemed speak of his loving kindness. The Lord sent the gospel in plainness so the weak could prepare, and these commandments now go to all. Those who will not hear face darkness, because they rejected his servants.
dc-133.setting: Church leaders held a conference at Hiram, Ohio, on 1–2 November 1831 to plan publishing Joseph Smith’s revelations. On 1 November Joseph dictated a revelation to serve as the book’s preface, now section 1. A later history says he dictated this one on 3 November, after elders asked about preaching and gathering. One early copy is dated 2 November, but the Joseph Smith Papers editors favor Whitmer’s 3 November copy. It came to be called the appendix. It was first printed in 1833, but not in the Book of Commandments, whose printing was stopped by violence in Missouri.

verse.text: Go ye out from among the nations, even from Babylon, from the midst of wickedness, which is spiritual Babylon.

dc-134.summary: This is a declaration of belief, not a revelation; each paragraph begins “We believe”. It says God instituted governments and holds people accountable for how they make and run laws. Good laws must protect conscience, property, and life. People must sustain the governments that protect their rights, and sedition is condemned. Civil officers should punish crime but never control conscience, and no religion should be favored by the state. Churches may discipline members only by removing fellowship, never by taking property or life. People should appeal to the law for wrongs, but may defend themselves when the law cannot act in time. The last paragraph says preaching to enslaved people against their masters’ wishes is unlawful and dangerous.
dc-134.setting: A general assembly of Church members met in Kirtland, Ohio, on 17 August 1835 and accepted the first edition of the Doctrine and Covenants. Oliver Cowdery and William W. Phelps then presented this declaration, and the assembly voted to print it in the book. Joseph Smith was away in Michigan Territory, and the author is uncertain; Cowdery may have written most of it. The Saints’ 1833 expulsion from Jackson County, Missouri, was a main reason for it. The JSP links the last paragraph to Missouri charges that the Church favored abolition.

verse.text: We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it, unless their religious opinions prompt them to infringe upon the rights and liberties of others; but we do not believe that human law has a right to interfere in prescribing rules of worship to bind the consciences of men, nor dictate forms for public or private devotion; that the civil magistrate should restrain crime, but never control conscience; should punish guilt, but never suppress the freedom of the soul.

dc-135.summary: This is not a revelation but a written announcement and tribute, speaking as “we”. It reports that Joseph and Hyrum Smith were shot at Carthage Jail by a mob of 150 to 200 men. It records their last words and says John Taylor was wounded and Willard Richards escaped. It then praises Joseph Smith’s work, including the Book of Mormon and the revelations in this book. It quotes Joseph saying he went “like a lamb to the slaughter” with a clear conscience. It adds that Hyrum read a passage from Ether 12 before leaving for Carthage. It gives the brothers’ ages and calls them martyrs. It ends by saying their innocent blood, on Carthage jail, Illinois, and the nation, is a witness to the gospel. That blood will cry to the Lord until he avenges it.
dc-135.setting: Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum were shot by a mob at the jail in Carthage, Illinois, on 27 June 1844. John Taylor was wounded, and Willard Richards escaped unhurt. This statement was written soon after and placed at the end of the 1844 edition of the Doctrine and Covenants. That edition was nearly ready for printing in Nauvoo when the killings happened. The official heading names no author, but the statement is traditionally attributed to John Taylor.

verse.text: Joseph Smith, the Prophet and Seer of the Lord, has done more, save Jesus only, for the salvation of men in this world, than any other man that ever lived in it. In the short space of twenty years, he has brought forth the Book of Mormon, which he translated by the gift and power of God, and has been the means of publishing it on two continents; has sent the fulness of the everlasting gospel, which it contained, to the four quarters of the earth; has brought forth the revelations and commandments which compose this book of Doctrine and Covenants, and many other wise documents and instructions for the benefit of the children of men; gathered many thousands of the Latter-day Saints, founded a great city, and left a fame and name that cannot be slain. He lived great, and he died great in the eyes of God and his people; and like most of the Lord's anointed in ancient times, has sealed his mission and his works with his own blood; and so has his brother Hyrum. In life they were not divided, and in death they were not separated!

routes.title: Joseph and Hyrum Smith go to Carthage

dc-136.summary: The revelation calls itself “the Word and Will of the Lord” for the camp traveling west. It orders the people into companies with captains of hundreds, fifties, and tens, under the Twelve Apostles. Each company covenants to keep the commandments, gathers supplies, and cares for the poor and widows. Pioneers are to go ahead and plant crops for those who follow. It names Ezra T. Benson, Erastus Snow, Orson Pratt, Wilford Woodruff, Amasa Lyman, and George A. Smith to organize companies. Then it gives rules for daily conduct: keep pledges, stop quarreling, return what is borrowed, and praise the Lord. It says the people must be tried, and calls Joseph Smith’s death needed to seal his testimony.
dc-136.setting: The Saints had left Nauvoo in 1846 and wintered on the Missouri River. Brigham Young gave this revelation at Winter Quarters on 14 January 1847. The camp was near Council Bluffs, on Omaha land, and planning the spring trek west. The revelation set out how the companies would be organized and prepared.

verse.text: My people must be tried in all things, that they may be prepared to receive the glory that I have for them, even the glory of Zion; and he that will not bear chastisement is not worthy of my kingdom.

dc-137.summary: This is a vision told in the first person by Joseph Smith. He says the heavens opened and he saw the celestial kingdom, its gate, and the throne of the Father and the Son. He saw Adam, Abraham, his father and mother, and his brother Alvin. He wondered how Alvin was there, since Alvin died before being baptized. The voice of the Lord answered him. Those who died without the gospel, but would have received it, will inherit the celestial kingdom. The Lord will judge all by their works and the desires of their hearts. Joseph also saw that children who die before accountability are saved there.
dc-137.setting: On the evening of 21 January 1836, Church leaders met on the top floor of the unfinished Kirtland temple. They were washing and anointing one another in preparation for the temple’s dedication. Joseph Smith’s father anointed him, and Joseph then reported visions of the celestial kingdom. His scribe Warren Parrish wrote the account in Joseph’s journal.

verse.text: For I, the Lord, will judge all men according to their works, according to the desire of their hearts.

dc-138.summary: This is a vision told in the first person by Joseph F. Smith. While pondering 1 Peter 3 and 4, he saw the faithful dead waiting for the Son of God. Christ appeared to them and preached the gospel, but he did not go to the wicked. Smith wondered how so much could be done in so short a time. He saw that Christ organized faithful spirits as messengers to teach the rest. He names many in that assembly, from Adam and Eve to Malachi, and saw Joseph and Hyrum Smith and other latter-day leaders among the dead. He saw that faithful elders continue this preaching after death. The dead who repent will be redeemed through temple ordinances.
dc-138.setting: Joseph F. Smith, President of the Church, reported this vision in Salt Lake City on 3 October 1918. The next day he told general conference he had received divine communications in recent months. The account was written down right after the conference. On 31 October 1918, his counselors, the Twelve, and the Church Patriarch accepted it unanimously.

verse.text: But behold, from among the righteous, he organized his forces and appointed messengers, clothed with power and authority, and commissioned them to go forth and carry the light of the gospel to them that were in darkness, even to all the spirits of men; and thus was the gospel preached to the dead.

od1.summary: This is an official statement, often called the Manifesto, issued by President Wilford Woodruff. It denies reports that the Church was still teaching or performing plural marriages. Woodruff says he will submit to the federal laws against plural marriage and urges members to do the same. On 6 October 1890, general conference voted to accept it as authoritative and binding. Excerpts from three of Woodruff’s later addresses follow it. In them he says the Lord showed him that, without the change, temple work would stop and leaders would be jailed.
od1.setting: In the 1880s, federal laws made plural marriage a crime and targeted the Church’s property. The Edmunds-Tucker Act of 1887 disincorporated the Church and allowed seizure of its assets. Many Church leaders were jailed or went into hiding, and temples were at risk. In 1890 the Supreme Court upheld the seizure law. President Wilford Woodruff issued this statement on 24 September 1890.

od2.summary: This is a letter from the First Presidency announcing a revelation, dated 8 June 1978. It was signed by Spencer W. Kimball and his counselors, N. Eldon Tanner and Marion G. Romney. It reports that they prayed at length in the Upper Room of the Salt Lake Temple. They say a revelation confirmed that all worthy men may be ordained, without regard for race or color. The letter extends temple blessings with the priesthood, so worthy men may share them with their families. Local leaders are to interview each candidate for worthiness as usual. On 30 September 1978, general conference voted unanimously to accept it as the word and will of the Lord.
od2.setting: A few Black men were ordained to the priesthood in the Church’s early years, including Elijah Abel. In 1852 Brigham Young announced that men of Black African descent could not be ordained. Black men and women were also kept from temple endowments and sealings. Church records give no clear origin for the practice, and the Church now disavows past theories offered to explain it. The issue grew pressing in the 1970s, as the Church grew in Brazil and West Africa.

adam-ondi-ahman.summary: Three years before he died, Adam gathered his righteous descendants in the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman. He gave them his last blessing. D&C 116 names Spring Hill, Missouri, as Adam-ondi-Ahman.

verse.text: Three years previous to the death of Adam, he called Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, and Methuselah, who were all high priests, with the residue of his posterity who were righteous, into the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman, and there bestowed upon them his last blessing.

adam-ondi-ahman.dateNote: The Church chronology gives the order of these events, not their years.

ch-pioneers-arrive.summary: Brigham Young's vanguard company arrives after crossing the plains. Settlement of the valley begins.

ch-sunday-school.summary: Richard Ballantyne holds the first formal Sunday School of the Church in Salt Lake City.

ch-deseret-news.summary: The first newspaper in Utah begins publication.

ch-utah-territory.summary: The United States organizes the Territory of Utah. Brigham Young becomes its first governor.

ch-pearl-of-great-price-1851.summary: Franklin D. Richards publishes a pamphlet of Joseph Smith's writings for British members.

ch-plural-marriage-1852.summary: Orson Pratt publicly announces and defends the practice at Brigham Young's request.

ch-hong-kong-mission-1853.summary: Three missionaries sail to Hong Kong, an early mission far beyond Europe and America.

ch-handcarts.summary: Emigrants pull handcarts across the plains to Utah. Two late companies are caught by snow in Wyoming.

ch-utah-war.summary: A United States army marches on Utah Territory. The standoff ends without a major battle.

ch-mountain-meadows.summary: Latter-day Saint militiamen murder at least 120 members of the Baker–Fancher wagon train. It happens during the Utah War.

ch-tabernacle.summary: The Church builds a great domed hall for its meetings. It hosts general conference until 2000.

ch-young-women.summary: Brigham Young organizes a society for the young women of the Church.

ch-byu.summary: A school in Provo opens that later becomes Brigham Young University.

ch-st-george-temple.summary: The first temple completed in Utah opens in the southern settlements.

ch-brigham-young-dies.summary: The Church's second president dies after leading it for three decades.

ch-primary.summary: Aurelia Spencer Rogers organizes a weekly meeting to teach children.

ch-pearl-canonized.summary: Church members accept the revised Pearl of Great Price as scripture.

ch-salt-lake-temple.summary: After 40 years of building, the great granite temple is dedicated.

ch-utah-statehood.summary: After agreeing to outlaw polygamy, Utah is admitted as the 45th state.

ch-laie-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated in Hawaii, the first outside the continental United States.

ch-cardston-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated in Canada among the Latter-day Saint settlements of southern Alberta.

ch-bern-temple.summary: David O. McKay dedicates a temple near Bern, Switzerland. It is the Church's first in Europe.

ch-hamilton-temple.summary: A temple is completed near Hamilton, New Zealand.

ch-washington-temple.summary: A temple rises near the national capital, the first east of the Mississippi since Nauvoo.

ch-sao-paulo-temple.summary: Spencer W. Kimball dedicates a temple in São Paulo, Brazil.

ch-tokyo-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated in Tokyo, Japan.

ch-book-of-mormon-subtitle.summary: The Church adds the subtitle “Another Testament of Jesus Christ” to its editions.

ch-mexico-city-temple.summary: Gordon B. Hinckley dedicates a large temple in Mexico City.

ch-manila-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated for the fast-growing Church in the Philippines.

ch-johannesburg-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated in South Africa. Temples now stand on every inhabited continent.

ch-freiberg-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated at Freiberg in Communist East Germany.

ch-seoul-temple.summary: Gordon B. Hinckley dedicates a temple in Seoul, South Korea.

ch-family-proclamation.summary: Gordon B. Hinckley reads a proclamation on marriage and family at a general meeting.

ch-hong-kong-temple.summary: A temple is dedicated in Hong Kong, a year before its return to China.

ch-living-christ.summary: The fifteen apostles sign a written testimony of Jesus Christ.

ch-conference-center.summary: A 21,000-seat hall replaces the Tabernacle for general conference.

ch-perpetual-education-fund.summary: The Church begins a loan fund for the education of young members in poorer countries.

ch-nauvoo-temple.summary: A rebuilt temple is dedicated on the site of the original. The date marks Joseph Smith's death.

ch-accra-temple.summary: Gordon B. Hinckley dedicates the first temple in West Africa.

ch-kyiv-temple.summary: Thomas S. Monson dedicates a temple in Ukraine, in the former Soviet Union.

ch-missionary-age-2012.summary: Thomas S. Monson announces that young men and women may serve missions earlier. Missionary numbers surge.

ch-nelson-president.summary: A former heart surgeon serves as the Church's seventeenth president until his death in 2025.

ch-kinshasa-temple.summary: The first temple in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is dedicated.

ch-rome-temple.summary: A temple opens in Rome after its dedication in 2019.

ch-oaks-president.summary: After President Nelson's death, Dallin H. Oaks becomes the Church's eighteenth president.
